paper_title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Robot manipulation policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training (Khazatsky et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024). Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of the training data rather than with its volume alone. Lin et al. (2025) report that generalization follows power law in the number of training environments and objects, while additional demonstrations per environment saturate; experiments with DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) and π0.5 (Black et al., 2025a) show the same dependence on scene diversity (Section 4.1). Robot data, however, is costly to collect across many environments. DROID gathered 350 hours across 564 scenes over 12 months with 50 data collectors (Khazatsky et al., 2024), and generalist policies are still trained on pooled robot data: 970k demonstrations from Open XEmbodiment for OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024), and data from 7 robot configurations and 68 tasks together with Open X-Embodiment for π0 (Black et al., 2025b). Egocentric (first-person) human video can be recorded at scale without robot hardware (Hoque et al., 2026), and robot foundation models have begun to use it: GR00T N1 trains on human egocentric video alongside synthetic and real-robot data, and learns from this action-free video through latent actions (NVIDIA et al., 2025). Egocentric human video improves visual representations for manipulation (Majumdar et al., 2023; Nair et al., 2022; Radosavovic et al., 2022) and, when co-trained with small amount of robot data, improves policy generalization to new scenes, objects and tasks (Kareer et al., 2025, 2026; Qiu et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2025). Existing egocentric datasets were mostly collected to study daily-life activity (Grauman et al., 2022), kitchens (Damen et al., 2022; Li et al., 2018), or scripted and instrumented tasks, mostly in lab or tabletop settings (Hoque et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2022; Sener et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023b). Skilled manual work in real workplaces, such as bricklaying, wiring, plumbing, garment sewing, microsoldering, hair cutting or engine repair, involves tools, materials and multi-step procedures, and is not the primary focus of these collections. Ego-Exo4D (Grauman et al., 2024) targets skilled activity explicitly, with multi-view capture rig in 123 scene contexts. Egocentric-10K and Egocentric-100K (Build AI, 2025a,b) release head-mounted video of factory and manual labor at 10,000 and 100,405 hours. HubEgo-100K spans 30 work categories, of which manufacturing and assembly is one (5.4% of hours), and pairs every episode with perframe data from the phones inertial measurement unit (IMU) and with task types and machine-generated action and language annotations. HubEgo-100K is an egocentric video dataset of skilled work recorded in the wild, and it is built for diversity  (Fig. 1)  . Contributors record named, unscripted task with head-mounted phone during their own work, in their own workplace or home, with their own tools and materials. By skilled work we mean trade, craft and service tasks done as an occupation. This paper describes the first release, v1.0 (10,124 hours of 1080p video with synchronized inertial data from one head-mounted phone camera), and measures its diversity axis by axis (Fig. 10, Table 4): 12,227 contributors; 15,548 environments across 11 setting types, with 83% of hours in workplace settings and 17% in households; 30 work categories and 56 task types; 35 action families; machine-generated descriptions that use 1,429 verb and 3,709 noun lemmas; and 56 phone models. An environment is one contributors own setting of one type (their kitchen, their workshop), so environments of the same type are separate physical places recorded by different contributors, and their count is close stand-in for the number of sites (contributors who share workplace count once each). Hours are spread along these axes: no contributor accounts for more than 0.22% of hours. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: video Egocentric datasets. EPIC-KITCHENS (Damen et al., 2018, 2022) recorded unscripted activity in participants own kitchens with head-mounted cameras and introduced verb and noun classes for actions. EGTEA Gaze+ (Li et al., 2018) paired cooking video with gaze. Ego4D (Grauman et al., 2022) collected 3,670 hours of daily-life video from 931 camera wearers in 74 locations and defined benchmarks over episodic memory, hands and objects, and forecasting. Ego-Exo4D (Grauman et al., 2024) captured skilled activities from synchronized firstand third-person views. Assembly101 (Sener et al., 2022), HOI4D (Liu et al., 2022) and HoloAssist (Wang et al., 2023b) focus on procedural assembly, category-level hand-object interaction and guided tasks, respectively, with 3D hand annotations. EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) recorded 829 hours of tabletop manipulation with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. EgoVerse (Punamiya et al., 2026) pools egocentric demonstrations from academic and industry groups for robot learning, and Egocentric-10K and Egocentric-100K (Build AI, 2025a,b) release head-mounted video of manual labor. Robot datasets and generalist policies. Large robot datasets (Brohan et al., 2023; Khazatsky et al., 2024; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024) report the effect of data diversity on generalization, as does π0.5 (Black et al., 2025a). Lin et al. (2025) measured how imitation learning generalization scales with environments, objects and demonstrations, using Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023), the policy class also used in DROID. Generalist policies such as OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024) and π0 (Black et al., 2025b) are trained on pooled robot data, and GR00T N1 (NVIDIA et al., 2025) adds synthetic data and human video to the mixture. Human video for robot learning. Human video serves as source of supervision in several ways: pretrained visual representations (Dasari et al., 2023; Majumdar et al., 2023; Nair et al., 2022; Radosavovic et al., 2022), affordances and hand-object contact mined from video (Bahl et al., 2023; Srirama et al., 2024), retargeting of human hand motion (Bahl et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2022), co-training of policies on human and robot data (Kareer et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023a), latent-action pretraining (Ye et al., 2025), and vision-language-action (VLA) models pretrained on human video (Kareer et al., 2026; Long et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). We review their quantitative findings in Section 4. Comparison with existing datasets. Table 1 compares HubEgo-100K v1.0 with egocentric and manipulation datasets on the two axes of diversity that most sources report, the people who recorded the data and the places where it was recorded, using the numbers of each datasets paper, website or dataset card; where sources count hours over all camera views or disagree, the table notes it. Among the datasets in Table 1 that report the number of people, the others list 9 to 2,087 and v1.0 has 12,227 contributors  (Fig. 4)  . Each contributor records in their own workplace or home, which gives 15,548 environments across 11 setting types and 30 work categories; the other datasets in Table 1 report 45 to 610 kitchens, locations, scenes or rooms. Hours are spread over many contributors: the median contributor recorded 21.3 minutes (mean 49.7), and among the datasets in Table 1, Ego4D averages about 3.9 hours per camera wearer. v1.0 pairs this diversity with 1080p video, inertial data, task types and per-episode action and language annotations under CC BY 4.0. Section 5.1 goes through the axes one by one.

sections.title: 3.1 Data Collection
sections.content: Contributors record named task with head-mounted monocular camera (a phone) during their own work, in their own workplace or home  (Fig. 3)  . The task is named but not scripted, and there are no staged recording seslighting, clutter, tools and materials are those sions: of the workplace or home. Each recording stores the video together with the phones sensor streams. v1.0 was recorded on 56 phone models; 95.3% of hours come from iOS devices and the rest from Android devices. 99.1% of episodes use the ultra-wide lens, and the median diagonal field of view is 114.3 degrees. 26.2% of hours were recorded in the morning, 49.0% in the afternoon, 17.2% in the evening and 7.3% at night (local time, 0.3% unlabeled; Fig. 17).

Head-mount check. Footage that was not recorded with the phone worn on the head is detected from motion and camera signals and removed. 3. Dense temporal segmentation. vision-language model segments every recording in time, and only the segments in which the contributors hands perform the named task are kept. The model-estimated on-task share of each episode is stored with its annotations (on_task_share; 96.9% hours-weighted). 4. Hand-visibility gating. panel of two visionlanguage models describes each recording at one frame per second and labels every sampled frame as showing no hand, the left hand, the right hand, both hands, or unclear. frame counts as showing hand when at least one model reports one, and unclear frames count as showing none. Recordings in which the hands are mostly out of frame are dropped. Two further rules apply: recording must reach minimum share of sampled frames with both hands, and every long stretch without hands is cut out. The model-estimated shares of sampled frames with at least one hand and with both hands are stored in the catalog (hands_share, hands_share_both). 6 Fig. 7: Share of hours and number of environments per setting type. Gray: household; blue: workplace settings. 5. Privacy detection and cutting. Review models inspect one frame every 2 to 6 seconds and flag children, faces of other people and private text (documents, screens, cards, license plates). Every flagged frame of child, and every run of two or more flagged frames of face or private text, is cut out with 5second margin; segments with single flagged face or text frame are withheld (Section 3.4). 6. Episode assembly. Each remaining segment becomes an episode. Recordings made at 30 fps are stream-copied without re-encoding, starting at the first keyframe at or after the segment start, and their frames keep the recorded capture times. Recordings made at 60 fps are re-encoded to constant 30 fps (libx264, CRF 18, one keyframe every 30 frames); output frame is the source frame nearest to t0 + k/30 s. Segments longer than 30 minutes are split into equal parts. 7. Integrity and synchronization checks. For every episode the pipeline measures the median and maximum frame interval, counts the intervals longer than 1.5 times the nominal interval and the frames repeated by re-encoding, and computes the drift between the real duration and the frame count at 30 fps (median absolute drift 0.017 s). Sensor timestamps are re-expressed in nanoseconds from the first video frame of the episode, so video and sensors share one timeline (Section 3.5). These signals are stored per episode in the catalog. 8. Task rebalancing. Hours are rebalanced across the 56 task types so that no task type dominates; the median task type holds 69.5 hours. 9. Annotation and packaging. The annotation model labels every episode (Section 3.3), and the episodes are written as LeRobot v3 dataset with one MCAP file of native sensor streams per episode (Section 3.5). recording yields one episode per kept segment or part: v1.0 contains 41,688 recordings and 72,754 episodes, 1.75 episodes per recording on average, and every episode lasts at most 30 minutes. sections.content: HubEgo-100K is hosted at https://huggingface.co/ datasets/HubLabs/HubEgo-100K and licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0): it may be used, shared and adapted for any purpose, including commercially, with credit to HubEgo-100K, Hub Labs (Hub Data, Inc.). Access goes through short form with automatic approval. The catalog and annotation tables can be read without downloading video, and single episodes can be fetched individually. This paper describes v1.0 (10,124 hours); further data is released in versioned increments toward 100,000 hours with the same format, annotation schema and license, and release notes and per-version statistics are published on the dataset page. sections.title: 3.4 Privacy and Ethics
sections.content: Each contributor agreed that their recordings may be used to train and evaluate AI and robotics systems. Before release we removed: segments where child, another persons face or private text (documents, screens, cards, license plates) was detected, cut with 5-second margin; and recordings in which faces fill large share of the footage; episodes in which the video annotation detected minor; care tasks performed on another person; audio, location, device identifiers and contributor identity. Contributor and recording identifiers in the release are pseudonymous strings; the phone make and model are kept as capture metadata.

Every episode has one entry in each of five stores, all keyed by episode_index  (Fig. 9)  . Video: videos/observation.images.main/, one MP4 per episode, 1920 1080 H.264 at 30 fps. 84.1% of episodes (86.1% of hours) are the phones original stream copied without re-encoding; the rest were recorded at 60 fps and converted to 30 fps. sections.title:
4 Which Data Properties Matter:
Evidence and Measurements
sections.content: This section reviews the published evidence on six data properties. Table 3 sets selected findings next to the corresponding measurements on HubEgo-100K v1.0, which Section 5 reports in full. Numbers about other work are quoted from the cited papers; numbers about HubEgo100K are computed from the released tables and are hours-weighted unless noted. Several of the cited studies vary robot or hand-held-gripper demonstrations rather than egocentric human video (Black et al., 2025a; Khazatsky et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025); we use them to select the properties to measure.

sections.title: 4.1 Environment and Object Diversity
sections.content: Evidence. Lin et al. (2025) collected over 40,000 human demonstrations with hand-held grippers and executed more than 15,000 real-world rollouts to measure scaling in imitation learning. They report that the generalization performance of the policy follows roughly power-law relationship with the number of environments and objects and that the diversity of environments and objects is far more important than the absolute number of demonstrations. For 8, 16 and 32 environmentobject pairs, performance plateaus at 400, 800 and 1,600 demonstrations, about 50 per pair, and collecting in 32 environments with one object each and 50 demonstrations yields policy with about 90% success on new environments and objects. In their environment-by-object sweep (their Fig. 6), the normalized score on Pour Water with one object per environment rises from 0.14 with one training environment to 0.74 with sixteen, while with sixteen environments, adding objects per environment no longer helps (0.74 with one object, 0.73 with four). The authors recommend collecting in as many diverse environments as possible. power-law fit against the total number of demonstrations is weak (correlation coefficients = 0.62 and 0.79 for the two tasks in their Fig. 7). Robot datasets point the same way. DROID (Khaz9 atsky et al., 2024) contains 76k trajectories (350 hours) from 564 scenes and 52 buildings; co-training with DROID improves success by 22 points in distribution and 17 points out of distribution over the next best alternative, and size-matched subset with fewer scenes performs worse out of distribution, which the authors read as the strength of DROID lies in its size and especially in its diversity. Open X-Embodiment pools data from 22 robots and reports that RT-2-X, trained on the pooled data, improves emergent-skill success from 27.3% to 75.8% (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024), which is evidence for cross-embodiment training rather than for environment diversity. For π0.5, Black et al. (2025a) train on data from 3 to 104 locations at fixed number of unique samples and find that performance in unseen homes generally improves with more training locations, with the 104-location model approaching model trained on the test environments. Xie et al. (2024) find that factors well covered in training data, such as backgrounds, stop being bottleneck for generalization, while camera position remains the hardest factor. DexWild (Tao et al., 2025) reaches 68.5% success in unseen environments, nearly four times robot-only training, with human data from 93 environments; it also reports that too high human-to-robot ratio degrades performance, so robot data remains necessary for grounding. MimicPlay (Wang et al., 2023a) uses 10 minutes of human play per environment, which the authors equate to about 3 hours of teleoperation. LAPA (Ye et al., 2025) pretrains on human manipulation video through latent actions and outperforms VLA pretrained on robot data from Bridge. Among VLA pretraining efforts, EgoVLA (Yang et al., 2025) raises long-horizon success on unseen backgrounds from 11.21% to 28.79% in simulation, BeingH0 (Luo et al., 2026) reports real-robot gains of 10 to 45 points per task from human-video pretraining, and GR00T N1 (NVIDIA et al., 2025) includes 2,517 hours of human egocentric video in its pretraining mix. Kareer et al. (2026) find that human-to-robot transfer emerges once the VLA is pre-trained on sufficient scenes, tasks, and embodiments, nearly doubling performance on settings seen only in human data (for example 32% to 71%). Measured in HubEgo-100K. See Sections 5.1 Measured in HubEgo-100K. See Section 5.7. and 5.3.

sections.title: Video
sections.content: Evidence. R3M (Nair et al., 2022) pretrained on Ego4D improves success on 12 simulated manipulation tasks by over 20% compared to training from scratch and by over 10% compared to CLIP and MoCo; on real Franka arm with 20 demonstrations per task, it reaches 56% against 24% for CLIP, and the authors attribute part of the gain to the data itself (34% to 42% when switching from ImageNet to Ego4D under the same objective). MVP (Radosavovic et al., 2022), whose 4.5M pretraining images include 2.6M Ego4D frames, outperforms CLIP by up to 75% and supervised ImageNet pretraining by up to 81%, and notes that larger models require bigger datasets. VC-1 (Majumdar et al., 2023), trained on more than 4,000 hours of egocentric video, finds that scaling data size and diversity helps on average but not universally, and that adding diversity helps more than adding size. Dasari et al. (2023) report that ImageNet, Kinetics and 100 Days of Hands are competitive with Ego4D and that the image distribution matters more than size, caution that motivates curation (Section 4.3). For policies, EgoMimic (Kareer et al., 2025) reports that adding human embodiment data improves task score by 34 to 228% relative to robot data alone, and that 2 hours of robot data plus 1 hour of human data outperforms 3 hours of robot data (128 vs. 74 points), with 1,400 human demonstrations per hour against 135 robot demonstrations. Co-training with human data in Qiu et al. (2025) raises out-of-distribution success from 34.7% to 59.4%, and human demonstration takes 4.8 to 7.6 times less time to collect than humanoid teleoperation.

sections.title: 4.3 Hand Visibility and Curation
sections.content: Evidence. Hands are the interface between human demonstration and robot policy. Shan et al. (2020) built 100 Days of Hands from 131 days of internet footage with 100K annotated frames (189.6K hands) labeled with contact state. HaMeR (Pavlakos et al., 2024) reconstructs 3D hands as MANO meshes (Romero et al., 2017) from 2.7M training examples, of which only 5% come from in-the-wild datasets, and reports 2 to 3 times improvement in PCK@0.05 on in-the-wild data over prior work. VISOR (Darkhalil et al., 2022) provides dense hand-object segmentation for 36 hours of kitchen video. VRB (Bahl et al., 2023) learns affordances from human hand-object contact and reaches 57% average success against 25% for the next method; HRP (Srirama et al., 2024) injects hand, contact and active-object labels mined from 150K Ego4D videos into pretrained encoders and improves real-robot success by at least 15% across five tasks, raising an Ego4D-MAE baseline from 0.51 to 0.73. Direct evidence on curation comes from Long et al. (2026), who co-train VLA on robot data and action-free Ego4D video. Of 3,976 raw hours, camera-stability gate keeps 1,893 hours (48%) and an additional visible-hand gate keeps 975 hours (25%). Training with raw Ego4D clips underperforms the robot-only baseline, whereas the clips retained after both gates surpass it; the stability gate alone provides at most small improvement, and adding the visible-hand gate gives further gain. The reported differences are about one to two percentage points. Measured in HubEgo-100K. See Section 5.8.

sections.title: 4.4 Task Breadth and the Long Tail
sections.content: In RT-1 (Brohan et al., 2023), removing Evidence. 25% of the tasks while keeping 97% of the data achieves an equivalent generalization performance to reducing the dataset size by as much as 49%, and the authors conclude that data diversity is more essential than data quantity. BC-Z (Jang et al., 2021) scaled data collection to more than 100 tasks and performed 24 unseen tasks with 44% average success without demonstrations for them. VC-1 finds that adding different kind of data (navigation) to Ego4D helps more than adding more manipulation data (Majumdar et al., 2023), and EgoVLA reports that increasing the scale and diversity of human pretraining data consistently improves downstream performance (Yang et al., 2025). In the opposite direction, at fixed budget of 200K clips, Long et al. (2026) did not observe consistent gain from increasing scene, object or interaction diversity alone. Measured in HubEgo-100K. See Sections 5.2, 5.5 and 5.6.

sections.title: 4.5 Contributor Diversity
sections.content: Evidence. The evidence on the diversity of demonstrators is less direct than for environments. Ego4D made diversity of people, places, objects, and activities an explicit design goal and recruited 931 camera wearers, including occupations such as bakers, carpenters, landscapers and mechanics (Grauman et al., 2022). For robot imitation at small scale, the robomimic study (Mandlekar et al., 2021) finds that 300 demonstrations from six operators of varying proficiency yield lower success than 200 demonstrations from one experienced operator, and Belkhale et al. (2023) find that less consistent actions at given state are often associated with lower policy success. BC-Z (Jang et al., 2021) similarly observes that pooling data from several robots and operators makes single task harder to learn, and that pooling across many tasks overcomes this. No controlled study has yet varied the number of human demonstrators at fixed hours for egocentric pretraining; the per-contributor identifiers of HubEgo-100K make such study possible, for example with contributor-disjoint splits. Measured in HubEgo-100K. See Section 5.1. 4.

sections.title: Inertial Sensing
sections.content: Evidence. In Ego4D, 836 of the 3,670 hours include IMU data (Grauman et al., 2022). MMG-Ego4D (Gong et al., 2023) builds video, audio and IMU benchmark from about 202 hours of Ego4D and notes that video consumes 60 times more storage and 43 times more compute than IMU. IMU2CLIP (Moon et al., 2023) aligns IMU with video and text and raises IMU-based activity recognition on Ego4D from 23.23 to 45.15 F1. sections.title: 5.7 Episodes and Recordings
sections.content: v1.0 contains 10,124 hours and 1,093,194,072 frames of 1920 1080 video at 30 fps, recorded from the contributors head with an ultra-wide lens (Section 3.1). Episodes are long: the median is 4.9 minutes, the 90th percentile 21.4 minutes, and 72.8% of hours lie in episodes longer than 10 minutes (Fig. 11, left). Episodes cut from one recording share recording identifier and carry their start and end time within it, so longer procedures can be reassembled. The step-level instruction of each episode provides language target of the kind used in VLA pretraining.

sections.title: 5.8 Hand Visibility and On-Task Share
sections.content: Hand visibility and on-task share are model estimates: hand visibility is the share of sampled frames in which the model panel of the curation pipeline reports hand, and the on-task share comes from the temporal segmentation model (Section 3.2). The pipeline keeps the segments in which the contributors hands perform the task. Over all hours, at least one hand appears in modelestimated 94.7% of sampled frames and both hands in 76.3% (Fig. 2b); for the median episode the share with at least one hand is 95.8%. 70.6% of episodes, holding 83.0% of hours, show hand in at least 90% of their sampled frames. The model-estimated on-task share is 96.9% hours-weighted (median episode 98.9%; 39.1% of episodes are estimated to be entirely on task), and 92.2% of hours lie in episodes with an on-task share of at least 90% (Fig. 2c). Both estimates are stored per episode, so users can apply stricter thresholds. The model-estimated share of sampled frames with both hands varies by action: 91.0% for Peel & shell, 87.2% for Fasten & connect and 86.3% for Sew & thread, against 52.2% for Sweep & vacuum.

sections.title: 6 Applications
sections.content: GR00T N1 organizes its training data as data pyramid (NVIDIA et al., 2025): web data and human video form the base layer, which provides broad visual and behavioral priors, synthetic data the middle, and realrobot data the top, which grounds the model in realrobot execution. HubEgo-100K is intended for that base layer. The data is action-free; established ways to use such data for policy learning are co-training with small robot dataset, pretraining on human data followed by fine-tuning on robot data, and training visual encoder on the human data (Hoque et al., 2026). contributordisjoint train, validation and test split, stratified by task type, is available on request, so that evaluation measures generalization to unseen contributors and environments. 16 on recordings of trade work may automate parts of the trades shown. Contributors agreed to this use of their recordings, and the privacy measures of Section 3.4 are applied to every episode before release. After rebalancing, the task mix of v1.0 does not reflect how often each task occurs in the world, so models trained on it should be evaluated in the conditions in which they will be used.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented HubEgo-100K, an in-the-wild egocentric dataset of skilled work whose main property is diversity, and described its first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of unscripted work recorded by 12,227 contributors in 15,548 environments across 11 setting types, 30 work categories and 56 task types. We measured this diversity axis by axis; inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing. We related the design of the dataset to published evidence on environment and object diversity, egocentric human video, hand visibility, task breadth, contributor diversity and inertial sensing, and reported the corresponding measurement for each property from the released tables. The dataset, its catalog and its annotations are available under CC BY 4.0. Discussion and future work. Subsequent releases will extend HubEgo-100K to 100,000 hours (Section 3.6). The release layout is built to grow: later releases can add other capture setups as sibling folders of mono/ (Section 3.5), and annotation layers such as 3D hand pose and hand-object contact (Section 6) can be added per episode under the same episode_index key. Our next step is to train baselines on the data: visual encoders pretrained on HubEgo-100K and policies co-trained with robot data, evaluated on contributor-disjoint splits, to measure how the diversity reported here carries over to policy performance. Later versions of this paper will add these experiments and cover subsequent releases.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content: For what purpose was the dataset created? Robots that manipulate objects in homes and workplaces need training data that covers the variety of those places, objects and tasks. Existing egocentric datasets focus mostly on daily-life activity, kitchens, or scripted and instrumented tasks. HubEgo-100K was created to provide egocentric video of skilled manual work (for example bricklaying, wiring, plumbing, garment sewing, microsoldering, hair cutting or engine repair), recorded by contributors in their own workplaces and homes. It is intended for research and development of perception, representation learning, action understanding and robot learning systems (Section 6). Who created the dataset and on behalf of which entity? Hub Labs (Hub Data, Inc., San Francisco, CA, USA). The authors of this paper are listed on its first page. All recordings are firstparty: every hour was recorded by Hub contributor, and the release contains no third-party episodes. Who funded the creation of the dataset? Hub Data, Inc.

sections.title: Composition
sections.content: What do the instances that comprise the dataset represent? An instance is an episode: continuous segment of head-mounted, egocentric video in which contributor performs named manual task, together with the phones sensor data and set of annotations. Episodes are cut from recordings; one recording can yield several episodes. Recordings and contributors are referenced by identifier (recording_id, contributor_id). How many instances are there in total? v1.0 contains 72,754 episodes from 41,688 recordings (1.75 episodes per recording on average), for 10,124 hours and 1,093,194,072 frames, recorded by 12,227 contributors. We count 15,548 environments, defined as distinct pairs of contributor and setting type (Section 3). The video totals 43.5 TB and the native sensor logs 1.29 TB. Does the dataset contain all possible instances or is it sample of instances from larger set? It is curated subset of what contributors recorded. The curation pipeline keeps the segments in which the contributors hands perform the task, privacy filtering removes content (see Preprocessing), and hours are rebalanced across task types so that no task type dominates. What data does each instance consist of? One MP4 video (1920 1080, H.264, 30 fps, monocular), the accelerometer and gyroscope reading at each frame in LeRobot v3 parquet, the native sensor streams in MCAP, one row in catalog.parquet and one row in meta/annotations.parquet (Section 3.5; fields in Appendix C). Episodes last at most 30 minutes (median 4.9 minutes). Is there label or target associated with each instance? Yes. Each episode has task type (56 types) in work category (30 categories); the task type is the task the contributor was asked to record. The annotation model adds, by dense video annotation, short free-text description, step-level instruction, an action family (35 families), skill group (18 groups), difficulty level (easy, medium or hard), setting type (11 types) and the share of the episode spent on task. meta/subtasks.parquet and meta/subtask_occurrences.parquet store the instruction of each episode in the LeRobot subtask layout. Is any information missing from individual instances? Four of the 72,754 episodes have empty annotation fields, 22 have no setting type and 209 have no time-of-day label. All episodes include accelerometer, gyroscope and device-motion data; the magnetometer and heading streams are present in 99.1% of episodes and the barometer in 93.6%. Audio, location, device identifiers and contributor identity were removed on purpose (see Preprocessing). Are relationships between individual instances made explicit? Yes. All tables are keyed by episode_index, the same identifier used in the LeRobot data and the videos. recording_id links episodes cut from the same recording, and recording_start_s and recording_end_s give the position of the episode inside it. contributor_id is stable across episodes and links all episodes of one contributor. Are there recommended data splits? We recommend contributor-disjoint train, validation and test splits, so that evaluation measures generalization to unseen contributors and environments; the identifiers needed to build them are in the catalog. contributor-disjoint split stratified by task type is available on request. Are there any errors, sources of noise, or redundancies in the dataset? (i) The annotations are machine-generated and have not been audited by human reviewers; hand visibility and on-task share are model estimates. (ii) 5.5% of episodes contain at least one frame interval longer than 1.5 times the nominal interval; the median absolute drift against the nominal frame rate is 0.017 over an episode and the 95th percentile 0.155 s; re-encoded episodes can contain duplicated frames. All three are logged per episode in the catalog. (iii) Native inertial rates differ by operating system: about 100 Hz on iOS devices and median of about 497 Hz on Android devices. (iv) Recordings come from 56 phone models, so the field of view varies across episodes, and camera calibration is not provided. (v) Video and inertial data share one timeline (Section 3.2); the 19 residual time offset between the camera and the inertial sensors has not been measured. Redundancy: several episodes can come from one recording, and 6.4% of the distinct descriptions are used by more than one episode. Is the dataset self-contained, or does it link to or otherwise rely on external resources? It is self-contained and hosted in one repository (https:// huggingface.co/datasets/HubLabs/HubEgo-100K). Reading it relies only on standard formats (MP4 with H.264, parquet, LeRobot v3, MCAP). Does the dataset contain data that might be considered confidential? The footage shows the inside of workplaces and homes. Segments in which private text was detected (documents, screens, cards, license plates) were cut out before release. Does the dataset contain data that, if viewed directly, might be offensive, insulting, threatening, or might otherwise cause anxiety? No. The footage shows manual work. Does the dataset identify any subpopulations (e.g., by age, gender)? No. The release contains no demographic attributes; contributors are identified only by pseudonymous identifier. Does the dataset contain data that might be considered sensitive in any way? The data is video of people at work in their own workplace or home. It contains no location data, no audio and no contributor identity. Care tasks performed on another person, episodes with detected minor and segments with private text were removed.

sections.title: Collection Process
sections.content: How was the data associated with each instance acquired? Video and sensor data were recorded by the contributors phone. The task type is the named task the contributor was asked to record. Descriptions, instructions, action family, skill group, difficulty, setting type and on-task share were produced by the annotation model, and hand-visibility shares were estimated by the model panel of the curation pipeline. What mechanisms or procedures were used to collect the data? Contributors record named, unscripted task with head-mounted phone during their own work, in their own workplace or home (Section 3.1). v1.0 was recorded on 56 phone models. If the dataset is sample from larger set, what was the sampling strategy? Curation followed by rebalancing: the pipeline keeps on-task segments, applies privacy filtering, and rebalances hours across task types. Who was involved in the data collection process and how were they compensated? 12,227 Hub contributors recorded the data. Contributors are compensated by Hub for their recordings. Over what timeframe was the data collected? The recording date of every episode is given in the catalog (recorded_date). Were any ethical review processes conducted? The dataset was collected by company and not as an institutional human-subjects study. Each contributor agreed to the use of their recordings (see below), and the privacy measures of Section 3.4 are applied to every episode before release. Did you collect the data from the individuals in question directly, or obtain it via third parties or other sources? Directly. Contributors recorded themselves at work; no third-party footage is included. Were the individuals in question notified about the data collection? Contributors made the recordings themselves for this purpose. Did the individuals in question consent to the collection and use of their data? Yes. Each contributor agreed that their recordings may be used to train and evaluate AI and robotics systems. Has an analysis of the potential impact of the dataset and its use on data subjects been conducted? The privacy measures of Section 3.4 limit the impact on contributors and on other people present during recording. Section 7 discusses the broader impact. Preprocessing, Cleaning and Labeling Was any preprocessing, cleaning or labeling of the data done? Yes, in the stages of Section 3.2  (Fig. 5)  : head-mount check that removes footage not worn on the head, dense temporal segmentation that keeps the segments where the contributors hands perform the task, hand-visibility gating, privacy detection and cutting (Section 3.4), episode assembly, integrity and synchronization checks, and rebalancing of hours across task types; human review decisions take precedence where available. Episodes recorded at 60 fps (15.9%) are re-encoded to 30 fps; the others keep the phones original video stream. Episodes are then annotated by the annotation model (Section 3.3). Was the raw data saved in addition to the preprocessed, cleaned or labeled data? The release keeps the phones original video stream for 84.1% of episodes and every native sensor sample of every episode in MCAP. The footage removed by curation and privacy filtering is not part of the release. Is the software that was used to preprocess, clean or label the data available? The curation and annotation pipeline is not released. Every statistic in this paper is computed from the released catalog and annotation tables, and the analysis script is available from the authors on request.

sections.title: Uses
sections.content: Has the dataset been used for any tasks already? This paper reports the statistical analysis of Section 5 and no model training results. Is there repository that links to any or all papers or systems that use the dataset? Not yet. What (other) tasks could the dataset be used for? Those of Section 6: visual representation pretraining, hand and hand-object pose, action recognition, VLA pretraining and cotraining, video prediction and world models, and visual-inertial odometry. Is there anything about the composition of the dataset or the way it was collected and preprocessed, cleaned or labeled that might impact future uses? See the answer on errors and sources of noise above. In addition, recorded time varies across contributors (the median contributor recorded 21.3 minutes), and task types were rebalanced, so their shares do not reflect how often the tasks occur in the world. sections.content: Will the dataset be distributed to third parties outside of the entity on behalf of which the dataset was created? Yes. It is distributed publicly, free of charge. Access goes through short form (name, organization, country, intended use) in which users agree to credit the dataset and may opt in to dataset updates. How will the dataset be distributed? Does the dataset have digital object identifier (DOI)? Through the Hugging Face Hub at https://huggingface.co/ datasets/HubLabs/HubEgo-100K, as LeRobot v3 dataset with MCAP sensor archives, per-episode catalog and annotation tables. Single episodes can be fetched without downloading the whole dataset. The dataset page is its reference address. When will the dataset be distributed? v1.0 is available on the dataset page. Will the dataset be distributed under copyright or other intellectual property (IP) license, and/or under applicable terms of use (ToU)? Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0, https:// creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/): free to use, share and adapt for any purpose, including commercially, with credit. sections.title: Maintenance
sections.content: Who will be supporting, hosting and maintaining the dataset? Hub Labs (Hub Data, Inc.) maintains the dataset; it is hosted on the Hugging Face Hub. How can the owner, curator or manager of the dataset be contacted? Through https://hub.xyz. Is there an erratum? No. Corrections are recorded in the release notes on the dataset page. Will the dataset be updated? Yes. Additional data is released in versioned increments toward the full 100,000 hours; each release keeps the same format, annotation schema and license, and release notes and per-version statistics are published on the dataset page. If the dataset relates to people, are there applicable limits on the retention of the data associated with the instances? The dataset is distributed without fixed end date. Will older versions of the dataset continue to be supported, hosted and maintained? Releases are versioned, and the statistics in this paper refer to v1.0. If others want to extend, augment, build on or contribute to the dataset, is there mechanism for them to do so? The CC BY 4.0 license allows anyone to adapt and build on the dataset with credit. Corrections and suggestions can be sent to the maintainers through the contact above. Task Types, Action Families and Skill Groups Tables 5 and 6 list the action families and skill groups of HubEgo100K v1.0 with their hours, and Table 7 lists the 56 task types.
